strengths: The paper tackles a concrete and important bottleneck in LLM-assisted program verification: high-quality supervision for loop invariant generation. The focus on data quality rather than only model scale is well motivated and useful.

The proposed WONDA pipeline is technically sensible: AST normalization addresses syntactic artifacts in verifier outputs, while LLM-based simplification is filtered through formal correctness and sufficiency checks. This gives the curated training labels a meaningful soundness guarantee, even though the LLM rewriting itself is heuristic.

The evaluation reports improvements across multiple SLM sizes and includes a stage-wise ablation over raw verifier outputs, normalized invariants, and simplified verified invariants. The V2 data consistently improves correctness, speedup rate, and VBP for the 4B and 8B models, with especially strong gains for Qwen3-4B.

The paper gives useful task definitions, verification semantics, prompts, algorithms, dataset statistics, training hyperparameters, sampling settings, and verifier configuration. Reproducibility is better than average if the claimed code, datasets, and models are actually released.

The contribution is practically relevant: a small fine-tuned model approaching the portfolio utility of much larger models on hard verification instances would be valuable for deployment where latency and cost matter.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate. The core recipe combines known ingredients: verifier-generated invariants, AST simplification, LLM rewriting, formal filtering, and supervised fine-tuning. The paper would be stronger if it more sharply distinguished WONDA from prior bootstrapping, invariant simplification, and verifier-in-the-loop data filtering approaches.

The evaluation scope is relatively narrow for the strength of the claims. The main test set is only 123 hard instances derived from InvBench/SV-COMP, and the paper does not clearly establish that training and evaluation programs are disjoint in source, families, or templates. This leaves a material risk of benchmark-family leakage or over-specialization.

The results are promising but not uniformly strong. For Qwen3-0.6B, V2 slightly reduces correctness relative to the base model, and timeout resolution remains very limited. Even the best model accelerates only about one quarter of hard instances, so the practical gains are meaningful but not transformative.

The VBP framing is useful but somewhat optimistic. It assumes a portfolio deployment where the verifier and LLM-assisted checks run in parallel, but the paper does not fully account for resource contention, orchestration cost, or the cost of running two verifier queries plus model inference in realistic settings. The latency-inclusive metric is helpful, but its definition appears to include model latency only for sufficient instances and needs clarification.

The comparison to large models is not fully satisfying. WONDA uses a powerful Kimi K2 Thinking model to generate simplifications for the training data, but the cost, availability, and contribution of this teacher model are not analyzed. It is also unclear whether Kimi itself, or the same simplification prompt at inference time, would be a stronger baseline.

Several methodological details need tightening: the threshold eta for verbosity, exact train/eval split construction, hyperparameter search protocol, number of generated candidates, random seeds, and statistical testing are either missing or only partially specified. Three runs with mean/std are helpful but insufficient to establish robustness across task order, sampling variability, and benchmark variants.

Some presentation issues weaken confidence. There is a typo/inconsistency in the discussion of Qwen3-8B speedup rates: the text says 8.5% to 10.7%, while Table 3 shows 10.8% to 21.7%. The impact statement is also quite minimal and dismisses negative societal impacts without discussing misuse or risks from automated verification errors in safety-critical settings.

The limitation discussion is brief. The paper should more directly address dependence on UAutomizer, generalization to other verifiers/languages/properties, cases where cast stripping changes semantics before later verification, and whether compact invariants can become less pedagogically useful when non-linear or solver-hostile expressions are introduced.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in program verification: generating loop invariants that are not merely valid but useful for accelerating a verifier. The distinction between correctness, sufficiency, compactness, and speedup is valuable and well motivated.

The WONDA pipeline is conceptually sensible: normalize raw verifier invariants, use an LLM to simplify/generalize them, then formally re-check candidates before using them as training data. This verifier-in-the-loop filtering is a strong design choice for soundness of the curated labels.

The experiments include ablations over raw, normalized, and simplified datasets, and report multiple practically relevant metrics, including correctness, speedup rate, mean speedup, and virtual best performance.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, prompts, training hyperparameters, sampling parameters, and UAutomizer configuration, which improves reproducibility relative to many LLM-for-code papers.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The strongest result is on only 123 hard instances, with speedup rates around 21.7-24.7% for the best fine-tuned models and only about 2-3 baseline timeouts solved per run. This is useful, but not enough to justify claims such as approaching GPT-5.2 or substantially accelerating verification in general.

The VBP metric is optimistic and somewhat misleading as a central performance measure. It is a post-hoc virtual-best/oracle-style metric and excludes or only partially accounts for model generation latency, scheduling, and resource contention. The paper repeatedly calls the LLM a zero-risk augmentation, but an actual deployed portfolio would need a concrete execution policy and realistic end-to-end accounting.

There is a serious unresolved concern about train/evaluation separation. Both training and evaluation are described as coming from InvBench-related released programs or SV-COMP-derived tasks, but the paper does not provide a convincing deduplication or leakage analysis across programs, loop structures, invariant templates, or benchmark families.

The contribution is not very original methodologically. AST normalization, LLM rewriting, verifier filtering, and supervised fine-tuning are natural combinations of existing ideas. The paper would need stronger empirical evidence or deeper analysis to make this feel like more than a useful engineering pipeline.

The soundness discussion is uneven. Proposition 4.1 claims normalization is semantics-preserving, but the text then says cast stripping can break soundness. Although final candidates are reverified, the statement of the proposition and the boundary between sound normalization and heuristic simplification are not cleanly presented.

The comparison to large models is not fully convincing. The curated data is generated using Kimi K2 Thinking, but the cost and dependency of this teacher model are not analyzed. The paper compares fine-tuned SLMs against GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-5.2 at inference time while largely ignoring the cost and possible bias introduced by the stronger model used during data creation.

The evaluation is narrow: all experiments use UAutomizer as the verifier backend, one hardware setting, and a single benchmark construction. The conclusion itself says other backend verifiers remain future work, which limits the generality of the claimed acceleration.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence, including grammatical errors, inconsistent or mistaken result descriptions such as the Qwen3-8B speedup discussion, and occasional formatting problems in tables. These are not fatal alone, but they compound the sense that the empirical claims need tightening.

The limitations and impact discussion are too thin. The paper does not adequately discuss metric optimism, benchmark leakage risk, dependence on proprietary/frontier teacher models, backend-specific behavior, or the possibility that generated invariants may improve benchmark performance without improving broader verification capability.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and concrete bottleneck in LLM-assisted program verification: raw verifier-generated invariants are often correct but poor supervision signals. The framing around correctness, sufficiency, usefulness, and compactness is clear and useful.

WONDA is technically sensible: AST normalization is semantics-preserving for the stated rewrite rules, and the non-sound LLM simplification stage is guarded by verifier-based correctness and sufficiency checks. This makes the core data curation pipeline sound as a producer of training labels.

The empirical results are promising. On the hard InvBench-derived instances, fine-tuning on V2 substantially improves correctness and speedup rates for 4B/8B Qwen models, and the ablation shows that LLM simplification plus verification contributes much more than raw or merely normalized invariants.

The evaluation includes multiple model scales, strong LLM baselines, repeated runs with means/stds, end-to-end latency reporting, and ablations over V0/V1/V2. The paper also provides useful implementation details: prompts, training hyperparameters, UAutomizer configuration, hardware, timeout, and dataset statistics.

The contribution is practically significant for the verification community: small fine-tuned models matching the portfolio utility of much larger models could make LLM-assisted verification cheaper and easier to deploy.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is still based on a fairly narrow evaluation setting: one main verifier backend, one benchmark family derived from InvBench/SV-COMP, and only the hard split emphasized. Generalization to other verifiers, languages, invariant styles, and benchmark distributions is not established.

The training/evaluation separation needs stronger documentation. The paper says it uses InvBench training programs and an InvBench-released SV-COMP evaluation collection, but does not make the exact overlap/de-duplication checks sufficiently explicit. For code benchmarks, even near-duplicate leakage can materially affect fine-tuning results.

The VBP framing is useful but somewhat optimistic. It assumes parallel execution of baseline verification and invariant-assisted checks, largely abstracts away resource contention, scheduling costs, and deployment constraints, and may overstate practical gains relative to a fixed compute budget.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, saying the 4B model approaches GPT-5.2 is only true under selected VBP/VBP-E2E metrics; GPT-5.2 remains much stronger in validity, correctness, and speedup rates. The paper should phrase this more carefully.

There are presentation issues and a few inconsistencies. For example, the results text for Qwen3-8B appears to misstate the speedup-rate change, and the manuscript has several typos/grammar issues. These do not undermine the main idea but reduce clarity.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The paper notes future work on other verifiers and training methods, but it does not deeply discuss risks from incorrect deployment, benchmark overfitting, trust boundaries between LLM outputs and formal tools, or possible misuse/misinterpretation of verifier-validated but context-limited invariants.

Reproducibility is promising but not fully verifiable from the manuscript alone. The authors claim release of code, datasets, models, and harnesses, but the review version does not include enough concrete artifact identifiers or instructions to assess whether all results can be reproduced exactly.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in neural program verification: training data quality for loop invariant generation. The distinction between merely correct invariants and invariants that actually accelerate a verifier is well motivated and useful.

The proposed WONDA pipeline is technically sensible: AST normalization removes syntactic artifacts, LLM-based simplification targets semantic compactness, and all retained candidates are checked by a formal verifier for correctness and sufficiency. This makes the central training labels much more trustworthy than unfiltered LLM rewrites.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad across model families and scales. Results on InvBench hard instances show consistent gains from V2 curation over base, raw V0, and normalized V1 training, including sizeable improvements in correctness and speedup rates for Qwen3-4B/8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B.

The paper includes useful ablations, hard/easy split reporting, prompts, training hyperparameters, verifier configuration, and dataset statistics, which improves reproducibility and makes the source of improvements clearer.
The limitations section is honest about reliance on UAutomizer and the risk of inheriting solver bias. This is a real limitation, but the paper does not hide it.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate rather than high. The main contribution is a careful data curation and filtering pipeline using existing verifiers and LLM rewriting, not a fundamentally new invariant synthesis algorithm or learning objective.

The strongest claims are somewhat overstated. Phrases such as “provable quality guarantees” and matching frontier models rely on a specific verifier, benchmark split, and VBP/VBPE2E portfolio metric. The generated model still has modest absolute correctness on hard cases, and even the best systems resolve only a small number of baseline timeouts.

The evaluation depends heavily on UAutomizer both as the data source and as the verifier used for grading/evaluation. This raises concerns about verifier-specific optimization and limits evidence that the learned invariants generalize across verification backends.

The train/evaluation separation is not fully reassuring from the manuscript alone. Both data and InvBench are derived from SV-COMP-related sources, and the paper should more explicitly rule out overlap or near-duplicate programs/invariants between UAutomizer-derived training data and evaluation instances.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete. The paper says code is publicly available, but the review manuscript does not provide enough concrete artifact details, and the simplification stage depends on Kimi K2 Thinking, which may be difficult to reproduce exactly. The exact raw invariant extraction process is also only lightly specified.

The evaluation is relatively small for the headline comparisons: the hard split has 123 per-loop instances, three runs, and high variance in some VBP estimates. More statistical testing or broader benchmark coverage would strengthen confidence.

The ethics/impact statement is brief. While the work is largely beneficial, formal verification tools used in high-stakes settings can create overconfidence if users misunderstand verifier/model limitations; this deserved a more concrete discussion.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in neural-assisted program verification: training data quality for loop invariant generation. The distinction between merely correct invariants and invariants that actually accelerate verification is useful and well motivated.

The proposed pipeline is simple and plausible: normalize noisy verifier output, ask an LLM to produce compact semantic rewrites, and filter candidates with a verifier. The verifier-filtering step gives a soundness argument for retained invariants, assuming the verifier configuration is sound.

The empirical section covers several model families and includes ablations over raw verifier output, normalized output, and the full WONDA pipeline. The consistent V0/V1/V2 pattern is one of the stronger pieces of evidence in the paper.

The paper includes prompts, dataset statistics, UAutomizer configuration, training hyperparameters, and some benchmark characterization, which helps reproducibility relative to many LLM-for-verification papers.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated. The advertised 'provable quality guarantees' are mostly a consequence of post-hoc verifier filtering, not a guarantee of the LLM rewriting procedure or the data-curation method itself. In particular, normalization is claimed to be semantically preserving, but the method also strips integral casts, which the paper admits can break soundness.

The evaluation metrics make the headline comparisons look stronger than they are. VBP/VBPE2E use a virtual portfolio with fallback to the baseline verifier, so poor or failed LLM invariants are often hidden by construction. Claims such as matching GPT-5.2 or GPT-OSS-120B are therefore not evidence that the small model is comparable as an invariant generator; the reported correctness and speedup rates remain much lower than the frontier model in several cases.

The central improvement is modest in operational terms. On the hard split, the best model improves average end-to-end time from about 193s baseline to about 163s, solves only a few of the 20 timeout cases per run, and has speedup rates under 25% for most fine-tuned small models. This is useful but narrower than the framing suggests.

There is a serious reproducibility gap around data generation. The full pipeline depends on UAutomizer outputs and Kimi K2 Thinking for simplification, but the manuscript does not provide enough detail to regenerate the exact curated dataset, and the claimed public code is not accompanied by an identifiable anonymized link in the paper text.

The train/evaluation separation is not fully convincing. Both data and benchmarks are derived from prior verifier/SV-COMP style sources, but the paper does not clearly rule out overlap by program family, template, or near-duplicate structure. Expanding multi-loop programs into per-loop instances may also inflate effective sample size and understate dependence among examples.

The comparison to very large off-the-shelf and proprietary models is under-specified. It is unclear whether decoding budgets, prompting, retries, latency measurement, and hardware/API conditions are comparable. Since latency and portfolio behavior are central to the paper's claims, this weakens the evidence.

The ablation does not isolate the role of the LLM simplifier from simple verifier-filtered augmentation or other deterministic simplifications. A stronger study would compare against cheaper non-LLM simplification, more candidates from raw/normalized invariants, and training only on grade-3 speedup examples.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The paper briefly notes dependence on UAutomizer and solver bias, but does not adequately discuss risks from unsound verifier configurations, overflow/cast semantics, benchmark leakage, or the possibility that learned invariants may encourage misplaced trust in automated verification pipelines.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and important bottleneck in program verification: generating loop invariants that are not merely valid, but useful for reducing verifier runtime. This is a well-motivated problem with clear practical significance.

WONDA is technically coherent: the pipeline distinguishes syntactic normalization from semantic simplification, and the potentially unsound LLM rewriting step is followed by verifier-based correctness and sufficiency checks. This makes the soundness story stronger than many LLM-for-formal-methods papers.

The evaluation is broad and convincing. Results cover several model families and scales, include hard and easy splits, compare against large off-the-shelf models, and report not only invariant correctness but also speedup-oriented metrics such as Rspeedup, VBP, and VBPE2E.

The ablation study is a major strength. The V0/V1/V2 comparisons show that raw verifier outputs can hurt fine-tuning, AST normalization helps only partially, and the full WONDA pipeline produces the most consistent gains across Qwen3, Llama-3.1, and Mistral models.

The paper provides useful reproducibility details, including prompts, grading algorithms, dataset statistics, training hyperparameters, sampling settings, UAutomizer configuration, and hardware/configuration information. The stated public code release further improves reproducibility.

Presentation is generally clear. The paper explains the verification setup, the candidate invariant decision procedure, and the practical difference between correctness and speedup in a way that should be accessible to ML readers with some formal-methods background.
weaknesses: The central novelty is more in careful data curation and validation than in a fundamentally new learning method. AST cleanup, LLM rewriting, verifier filtering, and supervised fine-tuning are individually familiar components; the contribution is a strong integration rather than a major methodological leap.

The claim of “provable quality guarantees” is somewhat overstated. The pipeline guarantees that retained invariants pass the chosen verifier’s correctness and sufficiency checks, but it does not guarantee that the LLM simplification is semantics-preserving, nor does it address incompleteness or bias of the verifier beyond the assumed oracle model.

The evaluation depends heavily on UAutomizer both as the source of training invariants and as the verification oracle for filtering and evaluation. This is reasonable for a focused study, but it leaves open whether WONDA generalizes to other verifiers, richer invariant languages, or verification tasks where UAutomizer cannot generate useful seeds.

The manuscript does not make fully clear whether there is any overlap or near-duplication between the training programs inherited from Wei et al. and the InvBench/SV-COMP-derived evaluation programs. Given the small and structured benchmark domain, stronger discussion of train-test separation would improve confidence.

Some headline comparisons to frontier or very large models should be interpreted carefully. The small fine-tuned models match or approach GPT-OSS-120B/GPT-5.2 mainly on end-to-end verification time, while their invariant correctness remains substantially lower than GPT-5.2 in Table 3. The paper mostly acknowledges this, but the abstract/conclusion phrase the comparison quite strongly.

The hard benchmark is still modest in size: 123 per-loop hard instances from 72 programs, with only 20 baseline timeouts. The reported standard deviations help, but broader benchmark coverage would be needed before concluding that the method robustly changes the frontier of neural invariant generation.

The limitations section is honest but short. It mentions dependence on UAutomizer and lack of verifier feedback/reasoning supervision, but does not substantially discuss safety/ethics issues around automatically generated verification artifacts, possible misuse through false trust in generated invariants, or deployment assumptions.
